The problem

New plats reach the city as paper documents, CAD drawings and GPS data, and each one has to be digitized into the city's geodatabase before staff can rely on it. Done by hand, that conversion was repetitive and took more than three hours of work every week.

What I did

  • Built an AI-assisted automation for the plat digitization process.
  • Created and quality-checked thousands of easement, plat, and ROW records, converting paper, CAD, and GPS records into GIS data.
  • [ADD: how the automation works, step by step, in a sentence or two each]

What I found

The automation saves 3+ hours per week. [ADD: how you measured that, plus records processed, error rate, or what staff do with the output]

What I would do differently

I would time the manual process before building anything, so the savings rest on a measured baseline rather than an estimate. I would also write the workflow down from the start, so someone else on the team could run and maintain it without me.

Projects / Do highways raise crime? A Houston buffer analysis

Do highways raise crime? A Houston buffer analysis

Course
GEOG 312: Data Analysis in Geography
When
April 2026, project draft
Team
Mia Clark, Alex Beane, Matthew Caldwell, Eric Siaba
Tools
ArcGIS Pro, R
Data
Houston crime data, TxDOT highways, census block groups
Status
Draft

The problem

We asked what effect highways have on crime in a city. Our hypothesis was that fast, easy escape routes would mean more crime near highways.

What I did

I wrote the report's abstract and methods sections. The methods set out the GIS workflow below, from scoring the crime data to comparing the half-mile buffer against the whole city.

What the team did:

  • Scored geotagged Houston crime data by offense class and mapped it in ArcGIS Pro.
  • Estimated population under a highway buffer by turning census block groups into a dot-density layer, converting it to single points, and selecting by location.
  • Selected TxDOT highways inside the Houston city limits and built a 0.5-mile buffer around them.
  • Computed per capita crime rates in R and tested the difference with a chi-square test.

What we found

The 0.5-mile highway buffer covers 34.5% of Houston's land area but accounts for 50.1% of the total crime score. The per capita crime score near highways was 0.123 higher than in the rest of Houston, and the chi-square test reported a statistically significant difference.

This shows crime is concentrated near highways. It does not show that highways cause it: dense, commercial land tends to sit beside highways too.

What I would do differently

I would test the difference on crime counts first and treat the severity score as a second layer, and I would add land use and population density to the model so the result says more than "crime is near highways". Known limits of the draft that I would fix before calling it finished: the chi-square test was run on severity-weighted scores rather than counts, and the conclusion should name the alternative hypothesis, not the null.

Projects / Road and land-ownership data for 400,000 acres

Road and land-ownership data for 400,000 acres

Role
GIS Intern Technician
Employer
Roseburg Forest Products, Roseburg, Oregon
When
May to August 2025
Tools
ArcGIS Pro, ArcGIS Field Maps, SQL
Scale
18 townships, 400 datasets, 400,000 acres
Status
Delivered

The problem

Roseburg manages timberland across a 400,000-acre region. Logging teams needed accurate road maps to get around, road ownership information had to be easy to pull up, ownership records had to be checked against each other for conflicts before the business could rely on them, and stream data had to meet government regulations.

What I did

  • Digitized 18 townships of road data.
  • Used SQL to develop and manage 400 road ownership datasets.
  • Developed an automated system for finding land ownership conflicts across a 400,000-acre region.
  • Modeled and mapped 12,000 streams.
  • Collected several miles of road condition data with ArcGIS Field Maps.
  • Produced 12+ maps in ArcGIS Pro to aid company decision-making.

What I found

The digitized roads supported more efficient navigation for logging teams, and the SQL datasets gave faster data access. The stream modeling supported adherence to government regulations. The conflict system turned record-checking into a repeatable process: it reconciled boundaries, caught conflicts between records, and produced a result the business could act on.

Company data is not shown here.

What I would do differently

The biggest lesson was to check records against each other before anyone relies on them. Next time I would build that conflict check first, on day one, rather than after the data was assembled, so problems surface while the data is still being built.
